item.title: The Secret Behind Bedtime Stalling
item.description:
Sleep

The Secret Behind Bedtime Stalling

Your child's bedtime delay tactics may be a clumsy ask for connection.

Posted July 25, 2026

Key points
  • Bedtime stalling is often a bid for connection, not simply a refusal to sleep.
  • Children need connection before they can comfortably tolerate separation.
  • Predictable connection helps children feel secure and settle to sleep more easily.
  • Small moments of undivided attention can reduce bedtime battles and strengthen attachment.
Source: Vitaly Gariev / Unsplash

If you've ever found yourself saying, "Just go to sleep!" after your child has requested one more hug, one more story, one more sip of water, and one more existential question about dinosaurs or death, you're not alone.

Bedtime can be one of the most frustrating parts of parenting. After a long day, many of us (myself included) are racing toward the finish line, hoping for a few quiet moments before our own heads hit the pillow. But what if some of the behaviors we label as bedtime stalling have a deeper meaning?

For many children, bedtime is the one part of the day when they have a parent entirely to themselves. The bustle of school, work, sports, dinner, homework, and errands finally quiets. They instinctively want to hold onto that feeling of love, safety, and belonging for just one more story, one more kiss, or one more minute together.

Children need connection in order to tolerate separation.

It's no coincidence that children's biggest worries and deepest questions often emerge just as the lights go out. With no soccer practices to rush to, no lunches to pack, and no homework demanding attention, their external world finally becomes quiet enough for their inner world to be heard.

The child who spent the afternoon laughing with friends may suddenly burst into tears because they remembered their best friend was absent from school. Another may begin worrying about tomorrow's spelling test or ask whether you'll always be there to tuck them in. Even the feeling of missing someone often surfaces as children prepare for the first significant separation of every day: Sleep.

As adults, we associate certain emotions with familiar experiences. The smell of popcorn reminds us of the movies. A favorite song transports us back to high school. Children make similar associations. Bedtime becomes linked with the experience of separating from the people who help them feel most safe and regulated.

While this is especially common in young children, the need for connection before separation doesn't disappear with age. I recently spoke with the mother of a 19-year-old college student who crawled into bed just before midnight—not because she couldn't sleep, but because she suddenly found herself wondering what life would be like one day without her parents. Development changes, but our attachment needs don't simply vanish.

From a developmental perspective, bedtime represents a daily transition from togetherness to aloneness. For some children, that's an easy shift. For others, it can feel surprisingly vulnerable.

The request for "one more hug" isn't necessarily an attempt to manipulate parents or avoid sleep. More often, it's an attempt to stay connected.

Young children are still developing the language and emotional awareness to say, "I'm feeling anxious about separating from you" or "I need reassurance before I fall asleep." Instead, they ask for another story, another song, or another minute while you sit beside them.

Source: Ana Curcan / Unsplash

Understanding the emotional need behind the behavior doesn't mean abandoning healthy boundaries or allowing bedtime to become a two-hour negotiation. Rather, it invites us to respond thoughtfully instead of reactively. Children benefit from knowing that both things can be true: My parent understands my feelings, and bedtime is still bedtime.

One of the most powerful ways to reduce bedtime struggles is to build intentional moments of connection into everyday life. Children don't necessarily need hours of one-on-one time. They need moments of feeling seen.

Just 10 minutes of uninterrupted, child-led play each day can have an outsized impact. For older children, connection might look like sitting together before bedtime to talk, draw, shoot hoops, or simply exist without an agenda. Many families find that creating a predictable "connection time" about an hour before bed gives children a chance to share what has been building inside them before the bedtime routine begins.

If your child isn't naturally talkative, consider leading with your own stories rather than questions. Share something that made you laugh that day, something that challenged you, or something you're working toward. Stories often invite connection in ways direct questions cannot, creating space for children to volunteer what's on their minds.

Predictability itself is calming. When children know there will be time to connect every evening, they often become less driven to delay bedtime in order to create that opportunity themselves.

Connection also doesn't require adding more to your already full schedule. It can happen over breakfast, during the drive home from school, while folding laundry together, or in the few quiet minutes before lights out. Children don't measure connection in hours. They experience it in moments of undivided attention.

Ironically, slowing down at bedtime often helps children fall asleep more easily. When children feel emotionally secure, their nervous systems are better able to settle. Research consistently shows that warm, predictable bedtime routines are associated with better sleep quality, fewer bedtime difficulties, and stronger emotional and behavioral regulation. They also provide daily opportunities to strengthen the parent-child relationship.

Parents often assume connection is one more thing to squeeze into an already impossible schedule. In reality, connection isn't another item on the to-do list—it's the foundation that makes many other parts of parenting, including bedtime, go more smoothly.

Sometimes bedtime stalling isn't really about stalling at all.

Sometimes it's simply a child asking, "Before I let go of today, can I feel close to you for just a little bit longer?"
